title: The beloved in the room
hookLine: a woman has longed for a man she's only heard described; he stands in front of her, and nothing happens, until someone says, that's him
carry: pratyabhijna: recognize the Shiva already here
tomorrow: why would anyone carry rice pudding to a spring?
last: RASA: A TASTE OF THE AWARENESS CALLED SHIVA.

lines: HE STANDS IN FRONT OF HER.
cards: A young woman has fallen in love with a man she's never met. She's only heard about him: how kind he is, how he speaks, what he's done. She thinks about him all the time.
Then one day he comes to her house and stands right in front of her. And she feels nothing much; he's just a visitor. Until someone at her side leans over and says: that's him.
Everything changes, though not one thing in the room has moved. A teacher in Kashmir used that story to explain what he meant by recognition.

teach.b: The teacher is Utpaladeva, a Shaiva thinker of Kashmir, and the story comes, in paraphrase, from his work on recognition. That word is the key: pratyabhijna. Not finding something new.
Recognizing what's already in front of you. In his teaching, Shiva isn't far off. Shiva is the very awareness you're living in, the one who sees and knows, right now.
So the problem was never that God is missing.

teach.h: THE BELOVED ALREADY IN THE ROOM
teach.b: It's like the woman in the story: her beloved is standing in the room, and she's still longing, because she hasn't recognized him. Nothing needs to be brought in. Something needs to be seen.
Look at what makes the difference: someone at her side who says, that's him.
In Utpaladeva's tradition, that's the role of a teacher and of teaching. The teacher doesn't hand you a new self. The teacher points.
Notice the joy, too. She doesn't get a lecture on who he is.

The recognition itself is the delight. And Utpaladeva also wrote hymns to Shiva, full of longing and tenderness, and the two belong together: the more you see that he's here, the more there is to sing about.

The week's Kashmir has been building this way: a valley drained so a hidden thing could be seen, a history told without bending, a theater where the small self steps aside, and now a woman who simply recognizes who's in the room.

how: Students of Kashmir Shaivism study Utpaladeva's teaching on recognition with a teacher, and his hymns to Shiva are read and recited as devotion.

o: where Utpaladeva taught that we recognize Shiva, already here
where a teacher would give each student a brand-new self
where seekers had to travel far to find a hidden Shiva

games.q: Utpaladeva and recognition — tap the pairs.

s: for Utpaladeva, the path is about finding something brand new
it's recognition: seeing what's already here.
in the story, the woman's joy comes when someone says, that's him
nothing in the room moves; the recognition itself is the delight.
Utpaladeva was only a thinker and never wrote devotional hymns
he also wrote hymns to Shiva, full of longing and tenderness.

games.q: your roommate says, 'if God's already here, why would anyone need a teacher?' what's Utpaladeva's answer?
o: the teacher points, like the friend who said 'that's him', and you recognize.
the teacher hands you a new self that wasn't there before.
the teacher brings Shiva down to you from somewhere far away.
games.why: in pratyabhijna, Shiva is your own awareness. the teacher adds nothing new; the teacher points, so recognition can happen.

practice: Notice that you're aware: of sounds, of the breath, of the body sitting, without hunting for anything new. Whenever the mind goes looking somewhere else, come back and say quietly inside: already here.
If you pray, you can turn to God as already present, in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir. The valley where Utpaladeva taught recognition: the beloved is already in the room, and the teacher simply points. Today's word.

orig.note: pratyabhijna in Sanskrit, written in Devanagari: recognition, the name of Utpaladeva's teaching.

carryVoice: Carry this: pratyabhijna, recognize the Shiva already here. Recognition finds nothing new, only who was here all along. Rest well; more Kashmir tomorrow.

sources.ref: Utpaladeva, Ishvarapratyabhijnakarika (the analogy of the lover recognized), with commentary
